title: Ancient Greece’s eras
description: Greek history runs from Bronze Age palaces through a Dark Age, the Archaic and Classical ages and the Hellenistic age, until Rome took over.

facts.text: Greece’s Bronze Age palace kingdoms, first on Crete and then on the mainland, ended around 1200 BCE, when the Mycenaean civilization fell.
The period from about 1200 to about 800 BCE, after the Mycenaean palaces fell, is often called the Greek Dark Age.
The Archaic period, from about 800 BCE to 480 BCE, saw Greek city-states grow and colonies spread.
The Classical period ran from about 480 BCE to the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE.
The Classical age (480 to 323 BCE) lasted less than 160 years and began roughly 700 years after the Bronze Age palaces fell around 1200 BCE.
The Hellenistic age ran from Alexander’s death in 323 BCE to Rome’s conquest of Egypt, the last Hellenistic kingdom, in 30 BCE.
In 146 BCE Rome defeated the Greek Achaean League and destroyed Corinth, bringing mainland Greece under Roman control.

title: Mountains and sea
description: About four-fifths of Greece is mountainous, which split communities apart, while deep inlets and islands kept almost everyone near the sea, the easiest road.

facts.text: Mountains cover about four-fifths of Greece.
Mountains made overland travel hard, so Greek communities in separate valleys grew up apart and developed independently.
Athens and Thebes, less than 100 km (60 miles) apart, came to see each other as foreign rivals.
Arms of the sea reach so deep into Greece that only a small wedge of the interior is more than 80 km (50 miles) from the coast.
Greece today has more than 2,000 islands.
In Greece, mountains restricted travel over land, while the sea opened up wider horizons.
Lowland, the best farmland, makes up only about one-fifth of Greece.

title: The Minoans of Crete
description: A Bronze Age palace culture on Crete that traded widely, painted lively frescoes and wrote in the still-undeciphered Linear A.

facts.text: Minoan civilization on Crete flourished from about 3000 BCE to about 1100 BCE.
The Minoans traded across the Aegean and with Egypt and the Levant.
The palace at Knossos was decorated with wall paintings of dancing, sports and dolphins.
The Minoans’ main script, Linear A, has never been deciphered.
By the mid-15th century BCE the palace culture of Crete declined, amid disasters, unrest and growing Mycenaean influence.

title: Evans at Knossos
description: Arthur Evans dug Knossos from 1900, named the Minoans after the legendary King Minos, and rebuilt parts of the palace in concrete.

facts.text: The British archaeologist Arthur Evans began excavating Knossos, on Crete, in 1900 and uncovered a great palace.
In Greek myth, King Minos of Crete kept the Minotaur, half man and half bull, in a Labyrinth built by Daedalus.
The palace’s twisting maze of rooms and corridors led some archaeologists to link Knossos with the Labyrinth legend, a link many now doubt.
Arthur Evans named the civilization Minoan, after Minos, the legendary king of Crete.
From the 1920s, Evans’s team rebuilt parts of Knossos in reinforced concrete and had artists complete its frescoes from fragments.
The philosopher R. G. Collingwood joked that Knossos’s rebuilt architecture seemed to consist of garages and public lavatories.

title: The Mycenaeans
description: Warrior kingdoms of mainland Bronze Age Greece, ruled from fortified palaces such as Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns.

facts.text: Mycenaean Greece was organized around fortified palace centers ruled by kings, such as Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns.
Later Greeks called the Mycenaeans’ walls of huge stones Cyclopean, believing only the one-eyed giant Cyclopes could have moved them.
In 1876 Heinrich Schliemann found a gold funerary mask in a grave at Mycenae and believed it was Agamemnon’s; it is still called the Mask of Agamemnon.
The Mask of Agamemnon dates to about 1550-1500 BCE, roughly 300 years before Agamemnon would have lived, if he existed.
In legend, Agamemnon was the king of Mycenae who led the Greek army against Troy.

title: Linear B
description: Mycenaean palace records in Linear B, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952, turned out to be the oldest written Greek.

facts.text: In 1952 the British architect Michael Ventris deciphered Linear B, working with John Chadwick, and showed it recorded an early form of Greek, the oldest known written Greek.
Linear B tablets, dating from about 1400 to 1200 BCE, were used for palace administration, mostly to record inventories.
Linear B tablets have been found at Knossos on Crete as well as at Pylos, Mycenae and other mainland palaces.

title: The Trojan War legend
description: Greek legend told of a ten-year siege of Troy after Paris took Helen, ended by the trick of the wooden horse, which is not in the Iliad.

facts.text: In legend, the Trojan prince Paris took Helen, wife of Menelaus, and a Greek army led by Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, besieged Troy for ten years.
Later Greek authors dated the Trojan War to the 12th or 13th century BCE.
The wooden horse does not appear in Homer’s Iliad; it is mentioned in the Odyssey and told in detail in Virgil’s Aeneid.

title: Troy’s archaeology
description: Troy was a real city at Hisarlik in Turkey, with nine main layers; archaeology cannot confirm a ten-year war as Homer tells it.

facts.text: Troy stood at Hisarlik in northwestern Turkey, near the Dardanelles.
Frank Calvert dug at Hisarlik first and persuaded Heinrich Schliemann, who excavated there on a large scale from 1870.
The mound at Hisarlik holds nine main layers of settlement, known as Troy I to Troy IX.
Schliemann believed Homer’s Troy lay at the bottom of the mound; his ’Priam’s Treasure’ came from Troy II, about a thousand years too early.
Scholars have proposed Troy VI or Troy VIIa as Homer’s Troy; Troy VIIa was destroyed around 1200 BCE.
Archaeology suggests Troy did exist, but a conflict on the scale of Homer’s ten-year siege may never have happened.

title: Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey
description: Two epics: the Iliad, a few weeks of the Trojan War’s final year, and the Odyssey, Odysseus’s ten-year journey home; they were the heart of Greek education.

facts.text: The Iliad covers a few weeks in the final year of the Trojan War, centers on the anger of Achilles, and ends with Hector’s funeral, before Troy falls.
The Odyssey follows Odysseus, king of Ithaca, who spends 10 years trying to get home after the Trojan War.
Homer’s epics were the basis of Greek education and culture throughout the Classical age.
In Xenophon’s Symposium, Niceratus says his father made him learn all of Homer to become a good man, so he could recite the Iliad and Odyssey by heart.

title: The Homeric question
description: Whether one poet called Homer composed the epics or many singers shaped them in an oral tradition is still debated.

facts.text: Homer is thought to have lived in the 9th or 8th century BCE, if he was a single poet at all.
Some scholars think one poet, Homer, composed the Iliad and Odyssey; others think many people retold and revised them.
The Iliad and Odyssey grew out of a centuries-old oral tradition in which singers inherited phrases, scenes and plots and reshaped them in performance.
In the 1930s Milman Parry showed Homer’s epics came from an oral tradition; in Yugoslavia he recorded singers, including one who could not read performing an epic about as long as the Odyssey.
Homer’s epics repeat set phrases such as "swift-footed Achilles", building blocks that helped singers compose in performance.

title: The Greek Dark Age
description: After the palaces fell around 1200 BCE, writing vanished and population fell; the causes are debated, and finds like Lefkandi show the age was not empty.

facts.text: Around 1200 BCE the collapse struck the whole eastern Mediterranean: the Mycenaean palaces and the Hittite Empire both fell.
Suggested causes of the collapse include earthquakes, drought and raiders called the Sea Peoples, and no single cause explains it all.
When the palaces fell, Linear B writing was lost, and no written accounts from the Dark Age survive.
During the Dark Age, population and farming output fell, and many settlements were abandoned.
In the Dark Age iron came to replace bronze: bronze needed long-distance trade, but iron could be mined in Greece.
At Lefkandi on Euboea, a grave of about 1000 BCE, rich by any standard, held a Cypriot bronze vessel and gold, inside a large building.
Historians now think the Dark Age was less dark than once believed: Greek culture and trade carried on.

title: The Greek alphabet
description: In the 8th century BCE or earlier the Greeks adapted the Phoenician alphabet and turned spare consonant letters into vowels; it is the ancestor of European alphabets.

facts.text: The Greeks borrowed their alphabet from the Phoenicians through trade, in the 8th century BCE at the latest and probably earlier.
The Phoenician alphabet had letters only for consonants; vowels were left unwritten.
The Greeks turned five Phoenician consonant letters, aleph, he, yod, ayin and waw, into the vowels alpha, epsilon, iota, omicron and upsilon.
The word alphabet comes from alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters, which go back to Phoenician aleph ("ox") and beth ("house").
The earliest datable Greek alphabet inscriptions, from about 725 BCE, come from Athens and from the Greek colony on Ischia, an island off Italy.
An early Greek alphabet inscription scratched on a wine jug from Athens names the jug as a prize for the best dancer.
The Greek alphabet is the direct or indirect ancestor of all modern European alphabets, including the Latin and Cyrillic ones.

title: Greek colonies
description: From the 8th to the 6th century BCE Greeks founded independent colonies around the Mediterranean and Black Sea, seeking land, resources and trade.

facts.text: From the 8th to the 6th century BCE, Greeks founded many new cities along the coasts of the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.
Greeks left home to found colonies because of land shortage and growing populations, a lack of metals, timber and grain, and strife in their home cities.
Trade was usually the first step: Greek traders came first, and settlers often followed.
Colonies were politically independent of their mother cities, but they modeled themselves on the cities that founded them.
Greek cities along the coast of southern Italy were called Magna Graecia, "Great Greece"; the first, on Ischia and at Cumae, was founded about 750 BCE.
Corinth founded Syracuse, on Sicily, in 733 BCE.
Marseille began as Massalia, founded by Greeks from Phocaea about 600 BCE.
In Plato’s Phaedo, Socrates says that people living between the Pillars of Hercules (Gibraltar) and the river Phasis (on the Black Sea) live around the sea "like ants or frogs about a pond."

title: Myth, memory and evidence
description: Early Greece is pieced together from myths and epics that kept Bronze Age memories, checked against archaeology and deciphered writing.

facts.text: Mycenaean culture left a lasting legacy in later Greek myths and epic poetry.
The Iliad describes a helmet covered in boar’s tusks; such helmets have been found in Mycenaean-era graves, centuries before Homer.

title: The polis
description: A polis, or city-state, was an independent town with its surrounding countryside; there were over a thousand, most of them small.

facts.text: A polis, usually translated “city-state”, included an urban center and the countryside for some miles around, with its villages.
Each polis was independent of its neighbors, with its own government, and the Greek city-states never formed a permanent union.
Scholars have catalogued 1,035 Greek city-states of the Archaic and Classical periods, out of some 1,500 in all.
Most Greek city-states had no more than several hundred to a couple of thousand people; the island of Lesbos alone held five city-states.
The polis emerged around 750 BCE and remained the main form of Greek political organization until the Roman Empire.
The English word politics comes from Greek politikos, “of citizens”, from polis.

title: Acropolis and agora
description: A Greek town had a fortified high city (acropolis) and an open meeting place and market (agora).

facts.text: A Greek city-state’s town usually had a citadel on high ground, the acropolis, and a marketplace, the agora.
Acropolis means “high city”: a city’s fortified high ground, a refuge in war and home to its chief religious buildings.
The Mycenaeans built a palace on the Acropolis of Athens.
The agora was an open space for citizens’ religious, political, judicial, social and commercial business.
Agoras were often enclosed by stoas, covered colonnades that sometimes held shops.
Agoraphobia, the fear of open spaces, was coined in 1871 from the Greek agora.
Around 500 BCE Athenians marked the edge of their Agora with marble boundary stones inscribed “I am the boundary of the Agora.”

title: Kings, aristocrats, oligarchs and tyrants
description: Greek cities were ruled in different ways; a tyrant was a ruler who seized power, not necessarily a cruel one, like Cypselus of Corinth.

facts.text: Greek gave us the words: monarchy means “rule of one”, aristocracy rule by the “best”, and oligarchy “government by the few”.
A Greek tyrant seized power instead of inheriting it like a king; the title did not automatically mean cruel, and Greeks judged tyrants by how they ruled.
The Greek word tyrannos was probably borrowed from a language of Asia Minor, most likely Lydian.
In the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, tyrants took power in many city-states by rallying opposition to rule by a few aristocrats.
In the 8th and early 7th centuries BCE the Bacchiads, an aristocratic family, ruled Corinth and founded colonies including Syracuse.
Around 657 BCE Cypselus overthrew the Bacchiads, who ruled Corinth violently, with popular support and a favorable oracle from Delphi.
Cypselus was reputedly so popular that he ruled Corinth without a bodyguard.

title: Citizens and metics
description: Citizenship came by birth and belonged to men politically; metics were free resident foreigners who paid a special tax and rarely became citizens.

facts.text: A citizen in a Greek city-state could vote and owed taxes and military service.
In a polis only men had political rights, though women still counted as citizens legally, socially and religiously.
Citizenship normally came by birth to citizen parents; outsiders were only rarely granted it, even after generations of residence.
Metics were free resident foreigners, including freed slaves, found in most Greek states and most numerous in Athens; the law protected them.
Metic comes from Greek metoikos, “one who has changed his residence”.
In Athens metics paid a yearly tax of 12 drachmas for a man and 6 for an independent woman, and needed a citizen sponsor.
Metics in Athens could not own land or a house without a special grant.
Pasion, a former slave, became a great banker in 4th-century BCE Athens as a metic, and was later granted citizenship.

title: Slavery in the city-states
description: Chattel slavery was widespread in Greek city-states; slaves came mainly from war and raiding, were legally property and did every kind of work.

facts.text: Chattel slavery spread in Greece after about 600 BCE; by the 5th century BCE slaves were as much as a third of the people in some city-states.
War captives were an important source of slaves; pirates and raiders also seized non-Greeks to the north and east for sale in Greece.
Greeks also enslaved Greeks defeated in war, but not members of their own polis.
Slaves were their owners’ property; Aristotle called a slave “a live article of property”.
Slaves did all kinds of work: cooking, cleaning and fetching water, farming, crafts such as pottery and metalwork, and mining.
Slaves had the worst conditions in the mines, working narrow tunnels prone to landslides.
The silver mines at Laurium, in Athens’ territory of Attica, employed as many as 30,000 slaves.
In Classical Athens, public slaves owned by the city certified that its coins were genuine.
Some slaves won their freedom; a freed slave became a metic, a free resident who was not a citizen.

title: Hoplites and the phalanx
description: Citizen soldiers who bought their own armor fought shoulder to shoulder in the phalanx, each man relying on his neighbor's shield.

facts.text: A hoplite was a heavily armed Greek foot soldier who fought in close formation; hoplites appeared probably in the late 8th century BCE.
A hoplite wore a metal helmet, breastplate and greaves, carried his shield on the left forearm, and fought with a sword and a thrusting spear about 2 m (6 ft) long.
Hoplites paid for their own armor and weapons, so only men of some property could serve as hoplites.
Hoplites marched shoulder to shoulder in a rectangular formation called a phalanx, normally eight ranks deep.
The 7th-century BCE poet Archilochus praised a soldier who is “a short man firmly placed upon his legs”, not to be uprooted from his spot.
Thucydides wrote that armies drifted right going into battle, as each man sheltered his unarmed side behind the shield of the man on his right.

title: Greek coins
description: Coins began in Lydia; Greek city-states then minted their own, each with its own emblem, and the names obol and drachma recall earlier spit-money.

facts.text: The first coins were made in Lydia, in Asia Minor, in the second half of the 7th century BCE, from electrum, a mix of gold and silver.
Greeks once used metal spits as money; the coin name obol comes from obelos, “spit”.
Six obols made a drachma, a name that probably meant “a handful”, from a Greek word for grasp.
Each city-state stamped its own identity on its coins, along with its own festivals and patron gods.
The island city of Aegina struck silver coins stamped with a sea turtle, a symbol of its naval strength.
Aegina’s later coins show a land tortoise; the Art Institute of Chicago reads the change as a sign of sea power lost to Athens.
Athens’ silver coins, the “owls”, were made from Laurium silver and circulated throughout the Classical world.

title: The ancient Olympics
description: Panhellenic games for Zeus at Olympia every four years, protected by a truce that guaranteed safe travel.

facts.text: The Olympic Games were held every four years at Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus, traditionally from 776 BCE.
The first Olympic champion on record, Coroebus of Elis, was a cook who won the sprint in 776 BCE.
At first the only event was the stadion, a sprint of one length of the track, about 192 m (210 yards); it gave us the word stadium.
Olympic winners originally received no money, only a wreath of wild olive leaves.
The Games were open to freeborn Greek men, who competed naked; married women were not allowed to attend.
The Olympic Games were panhellenic: open to all Greeks, not just one city.
A truce of several weeks let athletes and spectators travel to and from Olympia safely, even while wars went on.
In 420 BCE Sparta was barred from the Olympics for sending hoplites into Lepreum during the truce, and fined two minae per soldier.

title: The Oracle at Delphi
description: At Delphi the Pythia spoke for Apollo; cities, colonists and kings consulted her, and her answers could be ambiguous.

facts.text: At Delphi, in the mountains of central Greece, a prophetess called the Pythia spoke the will of Apollo, seated on a sacred tripod.
The oracle worked only a limited number of days, and generous donors could jump to the head of the line.
Greeks planning a new colony most often asked Apollo at Delphi for approval first.
Priests wrote down the Pythia’s answers in verse that was often highly ambiguous.
Herodotus tells that Croesus of Lydia asked whether to attack Persia and was told he would destroy a great empire: it proved to be his own.

title: Many cities, one people
description: Independent and often rival city-states still saw themselves as one Greek people through shared language, gods, shrines and games.

facts.text: In Herodotus, the Athenians say all Greeks share kinship in blood and speech, shrines and sacrifices, and a like way of life.
Rival city-states still shared a language, religion and culture that gave Greeks a wider sense of belonging, seen at the Olympic Games.

title: Athena and Athens
description: The Greeks told that Athena won Athens from Poseidon with the olive tree; the city honored her with the owl and the Panathenaia.

facts.text: In the Greek myth of the contest for Athens, Poseidon made a salt-water spring from a rock (in some versions the first horse), and Athena planted the first olive tree.
In the myth Athena’s gift won, and she is associated above all with Athens, the city that took her name.
Athena was linked with the little owl, which became famous as the symbol of Athens.
The Panathenaia, Athena’s great festival each July, celebrated her birthday; every fourth year it was held with great splendor.
At the Panathenaia a new embroidered robe was presented to Athena.
Winners at the Panathenaic games received jars painted with Athena and filled with olive oil from her sacred trees.

title: Athens and Attica
description: Athens was an unusually large city-state that ruled all of Attica; all its citizens were Athenians.

facts.text: Athens ruled the whole region of Attica, an area remarkably large for a single city-state; it could have held several.
Athenian myth said the hero Theseus had united the towns of Attica into one state.
By the fifth century BCE, citizens from all over Attica were called Athenians, with the same civic rights and duties.

title: Solon’s debt reform
description: About 594 BCE Solon cancelled debts, freed Athenians enslaved for debt and banned loans secured on the person.

facts.text: Solon was archon, Athens’ chief official, about 594 BCE.
Before Solon, poor Athenians could borrow on the security of their own person and be enslaved for debt, some sold abroad.
Solon’s “shaking off of burdens” cancelled debts, freed enslaved debtors and banned loans secured on the borrower’s person.
In a poem, Solon boasted that he brought back to Athens many who had been sold into slavery.
After his reforms Solon left Athens, saying he would not return for ten years, rather than be pressed to change his laws.

title: Solon’s laws and classes
description: Solon replaced Draco’s harsh code, wrote laws on public boards, and ranked citizens by wealth instead of birth.

facts.text: Draco’s law code of about 621 BCE punished even trivial crimes with death, which is why harsh rules are called draconian.
Solon’s laws replaced Draco’s harsh code, except for Draco’s laws on homicide.
Solon’s laws were written on wooden boards called axones, displayed for the public.
Solon divided citizens into four classes by income, measured in produce; the top class harvested at least 500 measures a year.
Under Solon, political privilege depended on wealth, not noble birth, and higher classes could hold higher offices.
The poorest class, the thetes, were barred from office under Solon but kept their right to take part in the Assembly.

title: Cleisthenes and democracy
description: In 508-507 BCE Cleisthenes mixed Attica into ten new tribes and created the Council of 500, founding Athenian democracy.

facts.text: After Solon, Athens was ruled by the tyrant Peisistratus and then his son Hippias, whom the Spartan king Cleomenes expelled in 510 BCE.
In 508 BCE Isagoras, backed by Sparta, won the top office, but his rival Cleisthenes had the people’s support; Cleomenes and Isagoras were forced out.
In 508-507 BCE Cleisthenes replaced Athens’ four old tribes, based on descent, with ten new tribes.
Cleisthenes split Attica into city, coast and inland, and gave every tribe townships (demes) from all three, so tribes were less likely to follow local and family loyalties.
Under Cleisthenes, a citizen’s rights came from his deme, a township that kept its own citizen register.
Each of Cleisthenes’ ten tribes sent 50 men, aged at least 30 and chosen by lot each year, to the Council of 500.
The Council of 500 prepared the proposals that the Assembly debated and voted on.
Cleisthenes is regarded as the founder of Athenian democracy.
The word demokratia joins demos (people) and kratos (rule); it was coined in the middle of the 5th century BCE.

title: The Athenian Assembly
description: Male citizens met on the Pnyx to debate and vote by show of hands; any citizen could speak.

facts.text: The Athenian Assembly (ekklesia) was open to all male citizens aged 18 or over.
The Assembly met on the Pnyx, a rocky hill in Athens with room for about 6,000 citizens.
In the 4th century BCE the Assembly met four times in each tenth of the year, 40 meetings a year.
The Assembly had final control over policy and usually voted by show of hands, a simple majority deciding.
The herald of the Athenian Assembly repeatedly asked “Who wishes to address the assembly?”, welcoming even men who worked at a trade.
Aristophanes’ comedy the Acharnians shows the Pnyx empty while citizens in the marketplace dodge a rope smeared with red dye.
Because too few citizens came to the Assembly, Athens began paying citizens to attend in the early 4th century BCE.

title: Ostracism
description: Athenians could vote on potsherds to exile a powerful citizen for ten years, without losing his property.

facts.text: Each midwinter the Athenians voted, without debate, on whether to hold an ostracism some weeks later.
In an ostracism each citizen wrote a name on an ostrakon, a piece of broken pottery.
If enough votes were cast (6,000, in Plutarch’s account), the man named most had to leave Attica within 10 days and stay away 10 years.
A man who was ostracized kept his property.
Ostracism, credited to Cleisthenes, targeted a leading citizen who might threaten the state; Athens remembered how Peisistratus had made himself tyrant.
Ostracism was first used in 488-487 BCE and fell out of use after an ineffective vote, probably in 417 BCE.
Plutarch reports that an illiterate voter asked Aristides, not knowing him, to write “Aristides” on his sherd, because he was tired of hearing him called “the just.”
A well on the north slope of the Acropolis held 190 ostraka naming Themistocles, written by just fourteen hands and apparently prepared in advance.

title: Athenian juries and courts
description: Huge citizen juries chosen by lot decided cases without judges, with timed speeches and secret bronze ballots.

facts.text: Each year 6,000 volunteers, male citizens at least 30 years old, were chosen by lot for Athens’ jury courts.
An Athenian court had about 500 jurors for public cases and about 200 for private ones.
Athenian jurors judged both law and facts, and voted without discussing the case among themselves.
Pericles introduced pay for jury service; critics said it filled the juries with common people.
In Athenian courts, litigants usually spoke for themselves, though others could speak for a defendant.
Speeches in Athenian courts were timed with a water clock, the klepsydra, which was stopped while laws and documents were read out.
Each juror got two bronze ballots, one pierced (for the prosecutor) and one solid (for the defendant); a tie meant the defendant won.
The two ballots looked identical apart from the axle, so a juror could hide the ends with his fingers and vote in secret.
Athens’ large juries made intimidation and bribery harder.

title: Pericles
description: Pericles led Athens by winning election as general year after year; Thucydides called it democracy in name, rule by the first man in fact.

facts.text: Most Athenian officials were chosen by lot, but the ten generals (strategoi) and some financial officials were elected by vote.
Pericles was born about 495 BCE and died in 429 BCE.
After his chief rival was ostracized, Pericles was re-elected general every year for fifteen years, according to Plutarch.
Pericles’ power rested on continual re-election and on his reputation, according to Thucydides, for intelligence and incorruptibility.
In Pericles’ funeral oration, as Thucydides records it, Athens’ constitution favors the many instead of the few, which is why it is called a democracy.
Thucydides judged that under Pericles, Athens was a democracy in name but in fact government by its leading man.
Plutarch says Pericles’ head was long and out of proportion, so almost all his portraits show him in a helmet, and comic poets called him “squill-head.”

title: Why Athens built the Parthenon
description: After the Persian sack, Pericles rebuilt the Acropolis; the Parthenon honored Athena, held her gold and ivory statue and a league treasury, and later exploded in 1687.

facts.text: The Parthenon was built after the Acropolis was sacked during the wars between the Greeks and Persia.
Pericles directed a magnificent rebuilding program on the Acropolis, and the Parthenon was part of it.
Work on the Parthenon began in 447 BCE; it was finished by 438 BCE, and its outside decoration continued until 432 BCE.
The Parthenon’s pediments showed Athena’s birth and her contest with Poseidon.
The Parthenon also held the treasury of the Delian League, an alliance of Greek states led by Athens.
Plutarch reports that Pericles’ enemies accused him of spending the Greeks’ common treasure, moved from Delos, to gild and adorn Athens.
Inside the Parthenon stood a great gold and ivory statue of Athena by Phidias, dedicated in 438 BCE and now lost.
The Parthenon was later a Byzantine church, a Roman Catholic cathedral and then a mosque.
In 1687, during fighting between Venice and the Ottomans, gunpowder stored in the Parthenon exploded and destroyed the center of the building.

title: Who was left out of Athenian democracy
description: Only adult male citizens took part; women, metics and slaves were excluded.

facts.text: Athenian democracy was for adult male citizens; women, slaves and resident foreigners (metics) were excluded from politics.
In 451 or 450 BCE a law carried by Pericles limited Athenian citizenship to people with Athenian parents on both sides.
In Pericles’ funeral oration, as Thucydides gives it, widows are told that the greatest glory is to be least talked of among men.
Metics were free foreigners living in Athens, including freed slaves, and they made up a large part of its population.
Metics paid a yearly tax, could not acquire land or a house, and had no direct part in Athenian politics.
Athens practiced chattel slavery: enslaved people were owned as property, mostly foreigners captured in war or sold by traders.
In Athens, children born to enslaved parents were also enslaved.

title: Lot versus vote in Athens
description: Athens filled most offices by lot, which Aristotle called democratic, and elected only a few, like the generals.

facts.text: In Athens most officials were chosen by lot from 487-486 BCE, and so were the Council of 500 and the juries.
Aristotle wrote that appointing officials by lot is thought democratic, and electing them oligarchic.

title: Sparta and the helots
description: Sparta conquered Messenia and made its people helots, state-owned serfs who farmed for Spartans, freeing citizens to train for war while fearing revolt.

facts.text: Sparta lay in Laconia, in the southeastern Peloponnese, on the Eurotas river.
Sparta conquered neighboring Messenia around 735–715 BCE, gaining a large tract of fertile land and reducing its people to helots.
Helots were serfs owned by the Spartan state rather than by individual masters.
Helots worked the land and handed over half of their produce, leaving Spartan men free to train for war full-time.
Helots greatly outnumbered Spartan citizens, by some estimates about seven to one, and Spartans feared a helot revolt.
Each year, on taking office, Sparta’s ephors declared war on the helots, so a helot could be killed without religious guilt.

title: Sparta’s two kings
description: Sparta had two hereditary kings at once from two royal families, alongside five ephors serving one-year terms, a council of elders and a citizens’ assembly.

facts.text: Sparta had two hereditary kings at the same time, from two separate royal families.
Sparta had five ephors serving one-year terms, a council of elders that led the citizens’ assembly, and an assembly that voted by shouting.

title: Sparta through outsiders’ eyes
description: Spartans wrote little about themselves, so most of what we know comes from non-Spartan writers like Herodotus, Xenophon and Plutarch, some writing centuries later; archaeology can test their stories.

facts.text: Spartans wrote little about themselves; most accounts of Sparta come from non-Spartans such as Herodotus, Xenophon and Plutarch.
Plutarch lived from about 46 CE to after 119 CE, centuries after Sparta’s great days.
Plutarch wrote that Spartan elders inspected newborns and had weak ones left at a chasm at the foot of Mount Taygetus.
In 2007 an anthropologist who studied bones from a pit near Mount Taygetus found adolescents and adults aged 18 to 35, and no newborns.

title: The agoge
description: From age seven Spartan boys left home for the agoge, state training in barracks that ran to about thirty, with short rations and stealing encouraged.

facts.text: From the age of seven, Spartan boys entered the agoge, the state’s training system, and lived in barracks grouped by age, away from their families.
The agoge’s training and barracks life lasted until a Spartan man was about 30.
Spartan boys in the agoge got little food and were encouraged to steal more.
Xenophon says a Spartan boy caught stealing was beaten for stealing badly, that is, for being caught.

title: Spartan women
description: Spartan girls trained in athletics, and women could inherit and own land and ran estates, but they had no vote, office or place in the assembly.

facts.text: Later Greek writers told of a Spartan mother telling her son to come back with his shield or on it.
Spartan girls exercised like boys, running, wrestling and throwing the discus and javelin, though they were not trained for battle.
Xenophon says Sparta trained women’s bodies because strong parents would have stronger children.
Spartan women could inherit and own land, and with men so often away they ran homes, farms and estates.
Aristotle wrote that nearly two-fifths of Sparta’s land was owned by women, and he counted it among Sparta’s faults.
Spartan women could not vote, hold public office or attend the citizens’ assembly.
In 396 BCE the Spartan princess Cynisca won the Olympic four-horse chariot race as the team’s owner, the first woman to win an Olympic victory.

title: The Persian Empire
description: Persia’s Achaemenid Empire, begun by Cyrus the Great around 550 BCE, stretched from Egypt to the Indus, the largest empire yet, run through satrapies.

facts.text: The conquests of Cyrus the Great, beginning around 550 BCE, founded Persia’s Achaemenid Empire.
At its greatest, the Achaemenid Empire reached from Egypt to the Indus River and westward into parts of Greece, the largest empire the world had yet known.
Persia was divided into provinces called satrapies, each owing a fixed yearly tribute.

title: The Royal Road
description: Darius I’s Royal Road ran more than 2,400 km from Susa to Sardis; relay couriers covered it in nine days, and Herodotus’s praise of them is carved on a New York post office.

facts.text: Darius I built the Royal Road, running more than 2,400 km (1,500 miles) from Susa, the Persian capital, to Sardis near the Aegean coast.
Ordinary travelers took about three months to cover the Royal Road; royal messengers using relays did it in nine days.
Herodotus wrote that neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stopped the Persian royal couriers.
An adapted version of Herodotus’s words about Persian couriers is carved on New York’s James A. Farley Post Office; the US Postal Service has no official motto.

title: The Ionian Revolt
description: Greek cities of Ionia revolted against Persia in 499 BCE; Athens helped, Sardis burned, and Darius made Athens’s role his reason to invade Greece.

facts.text: In 499 BCE Greek cities of Ionia, on the coast of what is now Turkey, revolted against Persian rule; with help from Athens they burned Sardis, and the revolt was crushed by 494 BCE.
Darius I used Athens’s part in the Ionian Revolt as his reason to invade Greece in 490 BCE.
Herodotus says Darius ordered a servant to tell him three times at every dinner: “Master, remember the Athenians.”

title: The Battle of Marathon
description: In 490 BCE Athenians and Plataeans beat a larger Persian force at Marathon when Miltiades’ strong wings surrounded the Persian center; Sparta arrived too late.

facts.text: In September 490 BCE a Persian force landed on the plain of Marathon, about 40 km (25 miles) from Athens.
Asked for help, the Spartans said they could not march until the full moon.
At Marathon about 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans faced a larger Persian force.
The Athenian general Miltiades strengthened the wings of his line; the Persians pushed back the thin center and were surrounded as the wings turned inward.
Herodotus counted 6,400 Persian dead at Marathon and 192 Athenians.
Herodotus says 2,000 Spartans reached Attica on the third day after leaving Sparta, too late for the battle; they viewed the dead at Marathon, praised the Athenians and went home.

title: The Marathon runner
description: Herodotus records Pheidippides running from Athens to Sparta before the battle; the run from Marathon to Athens is a later legend that gave the marathon race its name.

facts.text: Herodotus records that Pheidippides ran from Athens to Sparta before the battle to ask for help, about 240 km (150 miles) in about two days.
The run from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory is not in Herodotus; it is a later legend.
The modern marathon race honors the legend of the run from Marathon to Athens.

title: Thermopylae
description: In 480 BCE about 7,000 Greeks under the Spartan king Leonidas held the narrow pass of Thermopylae against Xerxes for two days until a local showed the Persians a path; the last stand included far more than 300 Spartans.

facts.text: In 480 BCE Xerxes, son of Darius, invaded Greece by land.
Herodotus claimed Xerxes had more than 2.6 million fighting men; modern estimates run from about 70,000 to 300,000.
At Thermopylae the Greeks held a line only a few dozen yards wide between a steep hillside and the sea, where a small force could block a large army.
Leonidas, a Spartan king, led about 7,000 Greeks, including 300 Spartans, and held the pass for two days.
A local Greek, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass.
Leonidas sent most of the army away; his 300, some helots and about 1,100 Boeotians from Thespiae and Thebes stayed, held one more day, and many if not all were killed.
Herodotus says the Spartan Dieneces, told Persian arrows would hide the sun, replied that they would fight in the shade; Plutarch later gave the line to Leonidas.

title: Themistocles’ fleet
description: Themistocles persuaded Athens to spend a silver windfall on the navy, giving it 200 triremes, oared warships with bronze rams.

facts.text: When Athens’s state-owned silver mines struck a rich vein, Themistocles persuaded the Athenians to spend the windfall on the navy, giving Athens 200 triremes by 480 BCE.
A trireme carried about 170 rowers in three tiers and a bronze-covered ram at the bow.

title: The Battle of Salamis
description: In 480 BCE, with Athens evacuated and sacked, Themistocles lured a much larger Persian fleet into the narrow strait of Salamis, where Greek triremes rammed it to defeat.

facts.text: After Thermopylae, Athenians evacuated women and children to the Peloponnese, much of the population sheltered on the island of Salamis, and the Persians sacked Athens.
Themistocles sent Xerxes a false message, and the much larger Persian fleet attacked into the narrow strait between Salamis and the mainland, where its ships could hardly maneuver.
At Salamis the Greek triremes rammed the Persian ships; the Greeks sank about 300 Persian ships and lost about 40.
Herodotus says Xerxes watched the battle from the foot of a hill facing Salamis, with scribes noting who fought well.
Xerxes went home to Susa, and in 479 BCE a Greek victory on land at Plataea ended the Persian invasion.

title: The Delian League
description: Founded in 478 BCE against Persia with its treasury on Delos, the League’s tribute paid for a fleet Athens led; Athens stopped members leaving and moved the treasury home, turning the league into an empire.

facts.text: In 478 BCE Athens and many Greek cities formed the Delian League to protect themselves from Persia; its treasury was kept in the temple of Apollo on the island of Delos.
Athens supplied the League’s commanders and decided which members gave ships and which gave money.
Over time most members paid money instead of sending ships, and the tribute built and maintained the fleet Athens led.
Around 330 cities appear in the League’s surviving tribute lists.
When Naxos tried to leave the League, Athens attacked and forced it back in.
In 454 BCE Athens moved the League treasury from Delos to Athens, and the League became in effect an Athenian empire.
League money helped pay for Pericles’ rebuilding of Athens, including the Parthenon.

title: The Peloponnesian War
description: From 431 to 404 BCE Athens’s sea empire fought Sparta’s land alliance; plague struck Athens, and Sparta, with Persian aid, destroyed the Athenian fleet and won.

facts.text: From 431 to 404 BCE, for 27 years, Athens, leading the Delian League, fought Sparta, leading the Peloponnesian League.
In the Peloponnesian War, Athens had the stronger navy and Sparta’s alliance the stronger army on land.
Thucydides, who lived through the war and wrote its history, said its real cause was Athens’s growing power and the fear it caused in Sparta.
Under Pericles, Athens avoided Sparta’s stronger army, kept its people inside the city walls and relied on its navy.
In 430 BCE plague struck crowded Athens, killing an estimated 75,000 to 100,000 people, including Pericles; Thucydides caught it and survived.
Athens lost a huge expedition to Sicily in 415–413 BCE.
In 405 BCE the Spartan admiral Lysander, with much aid from Persia, destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami, and Athens surrendered in 404 BCE.
Xenophon says the victors tore down Athens’s walls to the music of flute girls, thinking that day the beginning of freedom for Greece.
Sparta’s peace terms disbanded the Delian League in 404 BCE.

title: From allies to rivals
description: Sparta and Athens fought Persia side by side, as the Serpent Column’s list of 31 cities records, then split into rival leagues and fought each other.

facts.text: After the victory at Plataea in 479 BCE, 31 Greek cities dedicated a gold tripod on a bronze column of three twisted snakes, listing their names, at Delphi.
The Serpent Column’s list of cities begins with Sparta (the Lacedaemonians), then Athens and Corinth.
The Spartan commander Pausanias first had the monument inscribed in his own name; the allies objected, and the cities’ names replaced it.
Constantine moved the Serpent Column to Constantinople’s Hippodrome, and it still stands in Istanbul, without its snake heads.

title: The twelve Olympians
description: The Greeks told of twelve great gods who lived on Mount Olympus, Greece’s highest peak. The lists varied, and the gods looked and behaved like people.

facts.text: Mount Olympus, at 2,917 m (9,570 feet), is the highest mountain in Greece, and the Greeks regarded it as the home of the gods and the site of Zeus’s throne.

Among the Olympians, Zeus was the sky and weather god with the thunderbolt, Poseidon ruled the sea, Hera was queen of the gods and goddess of marriage, and Demeter was goddess of grain and agriculture.
Hephaestus was the god of fire and a blacksmith who made weapons for the gods; Hermes was the messenger of the gods and protector of travelers and trade.

Lists of the twelve Olympians varied: one common list is Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes and Dionysus, while Hestia, goddess of the hearth, or Hades was sometimes included instead.
Greek religion believed in many gods in human form under one supreme god, and in literature Hera often appears as Zeus’s jealous, vindictive wife who persecuted the women he loved.

title: Zeus, king of the gods
description: In Greek myth Zeus escaped his father Cronus, who swallowed his children, overthrew the Titans with his brothers, wielded the Cyclopes’ thunderbolt, and took the sky when the brothers divided the world by lot.

facts.text: Cronus, king of the Titans, learned that one of his children was fated to overthrow him, so he swallowed each child his wife Rhea bore.
Rhea saved the infant Zeus by hiding him in a cave on Crete and giving Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes to swallow instead.
Zeus grew up, forced Cronus to disgorge his brothers and sisters, and with his brothers Hades and Poseidon defeated Cronus and the Titans.
According to Hesiod, the Cyclopes Brontes (Thunder), Steropes (Lightning) and Arges (Bright Flash) forged Zeus’s thunderbolt, Poseidon’s trident and a helmet of invisibility for Hades.
Zeus was the Greek sky and weather god, sender of thunder, lightning, rain and winds, and his traditional weapon was the thunderbolt.
After defeating the Titans, Zeus, Poseidon and Hades divided the world by lot: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the underworld.

title: Poseidon, god of sea and earthquakes
description: Poseidon ruled the sea, earthquakes and horses, carried the trident, and in myth punished lands he lost, such as Argos.

facts.text: Poseidon was god of the sea, and his weapon and main symbol was the trident, perhaps once a fish spear; the Romans identified him with Neptune.
Poseidon was also god of earthquakes, known by the epithet enosichthon, ’earth-shaker’, and god of horses; in some myths he created the horse.
Poseidon contested Argos with Hera and lost; in one version he flooded the land, and in the version Pausanias tells he made its rivers disappear, so they give no water except after rain.

title: Athena
description: Athena, born fully armed from Zeus’s head, was the goddess of war, handicraft and practical reason: strategy rather than Ares’ bloodlust.

facts.text: The Greeks told that Athena emerged from Zeus’s forehead fully grown, in armor and giving a battle cry; in one version Zeus had swallowed her pregnant mother, Metis, goddess of counsel.
Athena was a goddess of war, handicraft and practical reason, standing for the strategic side of war rather than Ares’ violence and bloodlust; she was patroness of spinning and weaving.
Athena’s owl became famous as the symbol of the city of Athens.

title: Apollo
description: Apollo, Artemis’s twin, born on Delos, carried the bow and the lyre and was a god of prophecy and healing, later linked with the Sun.

facts.text: Apollo and his twin sister, Artemis, were born on the island of Delos, children of Zeus and Leto.
Apollo’s attributes were the bow, standing for distance, death, terror and awe, and the lyre, standing for joy through music, poetry and dance; he was also a god of prophecy and healing.
Apollo’s name Phoebus means ’bright’ or ’pure’, and in time he came to be connected with the Sun.

title: The Greek underworld
description: Hades ruled the underworld that bore his name; Charon ferried the buried dead for a coin, Cerberus guarded the gate, and Persephone’s yearly stay below explained the seasons.

facts.text: Hades was the Greek god of the underworld, and his realm, the house of Hades, came to share his name; he was also called Pluto, ’Wealth’, perhaps because he gathered all living things into his treasury at death.
Charon ferried across the rivers Styx and Acheron the souls of the dead who had received burial rites, and his fare was the coin placed in the corpse’s mouth.
Cerberus, the watchdog of the underworld, usually had three heads (Hesiod gave him 50) and snakes on his back; he kept the living out and devoured anyone trying to escape.

Hades carried off Persephone, daughter of Demeter, while she gathered flowers; because she ate a pomegranate seed below, she spent a third of each year (in some versions more) with him, and Demeter’s grief in her absence left the fields barren.

title: Heracles and his labors
description: Heracles, Zeus’s son hounded by Hera, served Eurystheus at Tiryns; of ten labors, two were not counted, so they became twelve.

facts.text: Heracles was the son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmene, and Hera persecuted him; as a baby he strangled two serpents she sent to kill him in his cradle.
Driven mad by Hera, Heracles killed his wife, Megara, and their children.
After asking the oracle at Delphi where to live, Heracles was told to dwell in Tiryns, serving Eurystheus for twelve years and performing ten labors, after which he would become immortal.

Heracles’ first labor was to kill the Nemean lion, whose skin he wore ever after; his labors also included the nine-headed Hydra of Lerna, a wild boar and man-eating birds, and the last was fetching up Cerberus from the underworld.
Eurystheus refused to count two labors: the Hydra, because Iolaus helped, and the Augean stables, which Heracles cleaned in a day by diverting two rivers, because he did it for hire.
The Greeks told that after Heracles died, his divine part ascended to heaven and he became a god.

title: Perseus and Medusa
description: Perseus, cast adrift as a baby because of a prophecy, beheaded Medusa by watching her reflection, fulfilled the prophecy by accident and was said to have founded Mycenae.

facts.text: Acrisius of Argos was told he would be killed by his grandson, so he cast his daughter, Danae, and her baby son, Perseus, into the sea in a chest, which grounded on the island of Seriphus.
King Polydectes of Seriphus, who desired Danae, tricked Perseus into promising to bring him the head of Medusa.
Medusa was the most famous of the Gorgons and the only mortal one; she had snakes for hair, and anyone who looked at her face turned to stone.
Perseus had winged sandals, the cap of Hades that made him invisible and a curved sword, and he guided himself by Medusa’s reflection in a shield given him by Athena.
From Medusa’s severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus, and her head was given to Athena, who placed it on her aegis.
Perseus turned Polydectes and his supporters to stone, and later, throwing the discus, he accidentally struck and killed Acrisius.
Perseus was said to have founded Mycenae; Pausanias heard it was named after a myces, the cap of his scabbard that fell there, or a mushroom he picked.

title: Theseus and the Minotaur
description: Theseus of Athens ended Minos’s tribute by killing the Minotaur with Ariadne’s thread, which gave English the word clue; his forgotten sail cost his father’s life.

facts.text: To avenge his son Androgeos, killed by Athenians, Minos made Athens send seven youths and seven maidens to be devoured by the Minotaur, every ninth year in one version and every year in another.

When the third tribute came due, Theseus, son of King Aegeus of Athens (or of Poseidon), volunteered, and Minos’s daughter, Ariadne, helped him escape the Labyrinth with a thread after he killed the Minotaur.

The English word clue comes from clew, a ball of thread; its sense shifted because of the clew Ariadne gave Theseus, the spelling clue appears by the mid-1400s, and the sense ’that which points the way’ dates from the 1620s.

Theseus promised to hoist a white sail instead of the black one if he returned safely, but forgot; Aegeus, believing his son dead, killed himself, and in one version drowned himself in the sea, thereafter called the Aegean.

title: The voyage of Odysseus
description: On his way home Odysseus tricked and blinded Polyphemus, earning Poseidon’s anger, heard the Sirens tied to the mast and lost six men passing Scylla and Charybdis.

facts.text: Trapped in the cave of the Cyclops Polyphemus, Odysseus said his name was Noman and blinded him with a heated olive-wood stake; when Polyphemus cried that Noman was killing him, the other Cyclopes told him to pray to Poseidon and left.
Polyphemus was Poseidon’s son and prayed to him for revenge, and Poseidon delayed Odysseus’s homecoming with shipwrecks and other disasters; Odysseus reached home as the sole survivor.

The Sirens, part bird and part woman, lured sailors to destruction with their song (Homer has two); Odysseus stopped his crew’s ears with wax and had himself tied to the mast so he could not steer off course.

Scylla and Charybdis beset narrow waters so close together that no ship could pass without meeting one or both; Odysseus lost six men to Scylla, the pair was later placed in the Strait of Messina, and ’between Scylla and Charybdis’ means between two equally bad choices.

title: Myth and city
description: Greek myths were tied to real places: poets like Homer and Hesiod shaped the gods, and cities claimed heroes such as Theseus of Athens and Perseus of Mycenae.

facts.text: Greek religion had no clergy and no sacred books; priests simply looked after cults.

Herodotus wrote that Homer and Hesiod, who he supposed lived not more than 400 years before him, taught the Greeks the gods’ descent, gave them their names, set their spheres and described their forms.

Thucydides wrote that before Theseus, Attica was a set of independent townships, and that Theseus merged their councils into one at Athens; the state-funded Synoecia, or Feast of Union, dated from him.

title: Philosophy, the love of wisdom
description: The word philosophy comes from Greek philosophia, love of wisdom.

facts.text: The word philosophy comes from the Greek philosophia, “love of wisdom”: philo-, love, and sophia, wisdom.

title: Reasons, not only myths
description: The first Greek philosophers, in 6th-century BCE Ionia, looked for causes within nature and questioned traditional stories about the gods.

facts.text: The first Greek philosophers lived in Ionia, on the coast of Asia Minor (now Turkey), in the 6th century BCE.
Early Greek philosophers sought causes within nature itself, not in the whims of gods who acted like people; Thales is counted as the first.
In the 500s BCE Xenophanes complained that Homer and Hesiod gave the gods theft, adultery and deceit, things people are blamed for.
Xenophanes said that if horses or oxen had hands and could draw, they would draw gods that looked like horses and oxen.
Xenophanes noted that Ethiopians say their gods are snub-nosed and black, and Thracians that theirs are blue-eyed and red-haired.

title: Thales and the Milesians
description: Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes of Miletus each named a natural source of all things: water, the boundless, air.

facts.text: In Plato’s Theaetetus, Thales falls into a well while gazing at the stars, and a Thracian servant girl mocks him.
Thales lived in Miletus, a Greek city on the coast of what is now Turkey, in the early 6th century BCE.
According to Aristotle, Thales said water is the origin of all things and that the earth rests on water.
Aristotle guessed Thales chose water because the food of all creatures is moist and seeds are moist too.
Seneca reports that Thales explained earthquakes as the earth, floating on water like a boat, being rocked by rough water.
Thales’s earthquake theory gave a natural cause in place of the mythic one, an angry Poseidon shaking the earth.
Anaximander, a pupil or associate of Thales, said everything came from the apeiron, “the boundless”, not from water.
Anaximenes, a third thinker from Miletus, chose air: thinned it becomes fire; thickened, wind, cloud, water, earth and stone.

title: Pythagoras and his followers
description: Pythagoras led a rule-bound community at Croton that believed souls are reborn in animals and that numbers underlie the world.

facts.text: Xenophanes mocked Pythagoras for telling a man to stop beating a puppy because he recognized a dead friend’s soul in its voice.
Pythagoreans believed that after death a human soul is reborn in other animals, so all living things are kin.
Pythagoreans lived by strict rules: they wore white, entered temples barefoot and did not eat beans.
Pythagoras grew up on Samos and, about 530 BCE, moved to Croton, a Greek city in southern Italy, where he gathered followers.
Later tradition says that people who wanted to become Pythagoreans had to keep silent for five years.
Pythagoras seems to have written no books, so what we know of him comes from other, mostly later, writers.
The central musical harmonies, the octave, the fifth and the fourth, match the whole-number ratios 2 : 1, 3 : 2 and 4 : 3.
Pythagoreans taught that numbers are the key to the world, summed up as “all things are numbers”.
Babylonian tablets from about 1900–1600 BCE show knowledge of the Pythagorean theorem, and there is no evidence Pythagoras proved it.

title: How we know Socrates
description: Socrates wrote nothing; he is known mainly through his followers Plato and Xenophon.

facts.text: Socrates, who lived in Athens from about 470 to 399 BCE, wrote nothing; we know him mainly through Plato and Xenophon.

title: Socrates’ method of questioning
description: Socrates questioned people who seemed wise, testing their definitions until contradictions showed they did not know what they thought they knew.

facts.text: In Plato’s Apology, Chaerephon asked the oracle at Delphi if anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the answer was no one.
To test the oracle, Socrates questioned politicians, poets and craftsmen, and found they thought they knew things they did not.
Socrates concluded he was wiser only in one small way: what he did not know, he did not think he knew.
In Plato’s Laches, courage is defined as staying at your post, then as endurance of the soul; Socrates finds flaws, and it ends unresolved.
Socrates’ questioning, the elenchus, tested a person’s definitions to expose contradictions and false claims to knowledge.
Cicero wrote that Socrates first called philosophy down from the heavens into cities and homes, to ask about life, morals, good and evil.

title: The trial of Socrates
description: In 399 BCE Athens convicted Socrates of impiety and corrupting the young, by a narrow vote, and he died by drinking hemlock.

facts.text: Socrates was about 70 when Athens tried him in 399 BCE.
Socrates was charged with impiety, not honoring the city’s gods, and with corrupting the young; his accusers were Meletus, Anytus and Lycon.
Socrates was tried before a jury of about 500 Athenian citizens.
In Plato’s Apology, Socrates says he stuck to Athens like a gadfly to a big, sluggish horse that needed stinging awake.
After Athens lost its war with Sparta, the Thirty Tyrants, led by Critias, ruled the city in 404–403 BCE.
Critias had been a companion of Socrates, which brought Socrates suspicion, though an amnesty in 403 BCE had closed that era.
Socrates was found guilty; in Plato’s Apology he says that if 30 votes had gone the other way, he would have been acquitted.
Asked to propose a penalty, Socrates suggested free meals in the Prytaneum, an honor Athens gave Olympic victors; the jury chose death.
In Plato’s Crito, Socrates refuses his friends’ plan to get him out of prison, arguing that he must not break Athens’ laws.
Socrates was put to death by drinking hemlock; in Plato’s Phaedo the numbness rises from his legs until it reaches his heart.

title: Plato and the Academy
description: Plato, Socrates’ student, wrote dialogues starring Socrates and founded the Academy outside Athens in the 380s BCE.

facts.text: Plato, born in Athens around 428 BCE, was a student of Socrates and was deeply affected by his death.
Plato wrote dialogues, usually with Socrates as the main speaker.
In the 380s BCE Plato set up a school outside the walls of Athens, at a grove called the Akademeia: the Academy.
The English word academy comes from the Akademeia, the grove where Plato taught.

title: Plato’s cave and the Forms
description: In Plato’s allegory, prisoners take shadows for reality; the way out leads to the Forms, perfect models of which our world holds copies.

facts.text: In Plato’s Republic, prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows cast on a wall by a fire behind them, and take them for reality.
In the allegory, a freed prisoner is dazzled by the fire, then dragged up into sunlight, where he sees real things and finally the sun.
For Plato, the senses show imperfect copies; real knowledge reaches the Forms, such as Justice, Beauty and Equality, and the sun stands for the Good.
In the allegory, the prisoners laugh at the man who returns and would kill anyone who tried to free them, often read as a nod to Socrates’ death.

title: Aristotle’s range
description: Aristotle, Plato’s student for 20 years, studied logic, biology, ethics, politics and more, and argued with Plato about the Forms.

facts.text: Aristotle wrote on a vast range of subjects, including logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetry.
Aristotle, born in 384 BCE in Stagira, joined Plato’s Academy in 367 BCE, aged 17, and stayed 20 years as pupil and colleague.
Aristotle often argued against Plato’s theory of Forms, saying friends and truth are both dear but it is our duty to prefer the truth.
Aristotle returned to Athens in 335 BCE and set up his own school there, the Lyceum.
Aristotle created the first systematic treatment of correct reasoning: the first logic.
On the island of Lesbos, Aristotle studied animals, especially sea creatures; more than 500 species appear in his works.
Some of Aristotle’s unlikely-sounding stories about fish were proved right many centuries later.
Aristotle argued each virtue is a mean between too much and too little: courage lies between cowardice and rashness.
Aristotle wrote perhaps as many as 200 works; about 31 survive, and they read like lecture notes and drafts.

title: The Stoics
description: Zeno of Citium’s Stoics, named for the Painted Porch in Athens, held that virtue is the only true good and that reason can master the passions.

facts.text: Zeno of Citium came to Athens about 312 BCE and taught in the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch; his followers were named Stoics after it.
Stoicism was founded in Athens about 300 BCE.
The Stoics held that virtue is the only true good.
The Stoics saw strong emotions as errors of judgment that reason could correct.
Later Stoics included the Roman statesman Seneca, the former slave Epictetus and the emperor Marcus Aurelius.
The Stoics taught living in harmony with nature, guided by reason.

title: Epicurus and the Garden
description: Epicurus taught that the goal of life is pleasure, defined as freedom from pain and worry, and lived simply in his Garden.

facts.text: Epicurus opened his school, the Garden, in Athens around 306 BCE, and it admitted women and enslaved people.
Epicurus called pleasure the goal of life, defining it as the absence of pain in the body and trouble in the soul.
Epicurus’s school lived mainly on barley bread and water.
In a letter, Epicurus asked for a little pot of cheese so that he could have a feast when he liked.
Epicurus taught that death is nothing to us: while we exist, death is not here, and when death comes, we no longer exist.

title: Diogenes and the Cynics
description: Diogenes of Sinope, the Dog, lived in poverty, mocked convention and searched with a lamp for a real human being; his line runs to the Stoics.

facts.text: Diogenes Laertius says Diogenes lit a lamp in broad daylight and went about saying, “I am looking for a man.”
Tradition remembers the lamp as a search for an honest man.
Diogenes came from Sinope, a Greek city on the Black Sea coast, and was said to have been exiled for adulterating the coinage.
In Athens Diogenes lived in poverty, begged for food and slept in public places; he later lived in a large storage jar.
Cynic comes from the Greek for “dog-like”; Diogenes was called the Dog, probably for doing everything in public.
Diogenes taught that virtue meant living simply, according to nature, and rejecting empty customs and luxury.
When Plato defined a human as a featherless biped, Diogenes plucked a chicken, brought it in and said, “Here is Plato’s man.”
In a famous story, when Alexander the Great offered Diogenes any favor, he replied, “Stand out of my light.”
Asked where he came from, Diogenes said, “I am a citizen of the world.”
Diogenes taught Crates, and Crates taught Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.

title: A chain of teachers
description: Socrates taught Plato and Plato taught Aristotle; each learned from the one before and then argued his own way, all in Athens.

facts.text: Socrates taught Plato, and Plato taught Aristotle.

title: Euclid’s Elements
description: Euclid’s Elements built geometry by proving every result from a few stated starting points, a standard for proof that lasted over 2,000 years.

facts.text: Euclid, the most prominent mathematician of Greco-Roman antiquity, worked in Alexandria, Egypt, around 300 BCE.
Book I of Euclid’s Elements opens with 23 definitions, such as “A point is that which has no part”, then five postulates and five common notions, accepted without proof.
The Elements proves its results step by step from its definitions, postulates and common notions, setting a standard for deductive reasoning.
Euclid compiled the Elements from the work of earlier mathematicians, but the design of the whole work was his own.
The Elements has 13 books, covering plane geometry, numbers and solid (three-dimensional) figures.
More than 1,000 editions of the Elements have been published since it was first printed in 1482.
The Elements set a standard for proof and for teaching geometry that lasted, practically unchanged, for more than 2,000 years.
Proclus, writing centuries after Euclid, tells that King Ptolemy asked for a shorter way to geometry than the Elements; Euclid replied there was no royal road.

title: Archimedes: levers and floating
description: Archimedes of Syracuse found the law of the lever and the rule that an object in a fluid is lighter by the weight of fluid it displaces.

facts.text: Archimedes lived in Syracuse, on Sicily, from about 287 BCE until 212 or 211 BCE.
Archimedes showed that weights balance on a lever at distances from the pivot in inverse proportion to the weights.
“Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth” is quoted by Pappus of Alexandria around 340 CE; it is probably not Archimedes’ own words.
In On Floating Bodies, Archimedes showed that a solid denser than a fluid, immersed in it, is lighter by the weight of the fluid it displaces.
Vitruvius tells how Archimedes tested King Hiero’s gold wreath for silver; the water test is probably true, but the naked “Eureka!” run is later embellishment.
Archimedes’ war machines long delayed the Roman capture of Syracuse; when the city fell in 212 or 211 BCE, he was killed.

title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
description: Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s circumference from the noon Sun’s angle at Syene and Alexandria, using geometry and parallel rays.

facts.text: Eratosthenes, born in Cyrene about 276 BCE, settled in Alexandria and became director of its great library.
Eratosthenes was nicknamed Beta: good in many fields but second best in each, like an all-round athlete taking second prizes.
At noon on the summer solstice the Sun shone straight down at Syene, in southern Egypt, while at Alexandria it was about 7° from vertical, about 1/50 of a circle.
Eratosthenes assumed the Sun’s rays arrive parallel; by Euclid’s rule for a line crossing parallel lines, the angle at Alexandria equals the angle at Earth’s center.
Since the angle was 1/50 of a circle, the Syene to Alexandria distance was 1/50 of Earth’s circumference; Eratosthenes got 250,000 stadia.
How accurate Eratosthenes was depends on the length of his stadion; estimates of his error run from 0.5 to 17 percent.

title: Greek models of the heavens
description: Greek astronomers modeled the sky with circles and spheres, mostly around Earth; Aristarchus proposed a Sun-centered system, and Hipparchus found precession.

facts.text: Eudoxus of Cnidus (4th century BCE) modeled the heavens with 27 spheres around Earth: one for the stars, three each for Sun and Moon, four per planet.
Eudoxus’s rule that every heavenly motion is uniform and circular, endorsed by Aristotle, remained orthodox until Kepler in the 1600s.
Aristarchus of Samos (about 310 to 230 BCE) proposed that the Sun, not Earth, is at the center, with Earth moving around it.
Archimedes’ Sand-Reckoner gives the most detailed surviving description of Aristarchus’s idea, noting it would make the universe vastly larger.
The Sun-centered idea won little support: no one could see the stars shift as Earth moved, and Aristarchus’s answer, that the stars are immensely far away, couldn’t be tested.
Hipparchus, working in the 2nd century BCE, catalogued the positions of about 850 stars.
Comparing his observations with ones from the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE, Hipparchus found stars had shifted about 2°: the precession of the equinoxes.
Ptolemy’s Almagest, completed about 150 CE, kept Earth at the center and relied on Hipparchus’s work.

title: The Antikythera mechanism
description: A geared bronze calculator from about 100 BCE, found in a shipwreck, that showed the Sun, Moon and eclipses.

facts.text: In 1901 sponge divers recovered the Antikythera mechanism from the wreck of a trading ship that sank in the first half of the 1st century BCE.
The Antikythera mechanism was made around 100 BCE, give or take 30 years.
X-ray images showed that the surviving fragments contain 30 bronze gear wheels.
Turned by a hand crank, the mechanism showed the Sun and Moon in the zodiac, the Moon’s phases on a half-silvered ball, and predicted eclipses.
The Antikythera mechanism also showed when the Panhellenic games, including the ancient Olympic Games, would take place.
No geared mechanism as complex is known from the ancient world, or until medieval cathedral clocks about a thousand years later.

title: Hippocratic medicine
description: Hippocratic writers treated disease as natural, not divine, and recorded case histories, though theories like the four humors were wrong.

facts.text: Hippocrates lived from about 460 to about 375 BCE and worked on the island of Cos; Plato mentions him as an admired physician and teacher.
Facts about Hippocrates’ life are hard to separate from tales told about him later.
About 60 medical writings survive under Hippocrates’ name, and most of them were not written by him.
The Hippocratic On the Sacred Disease says epilepsy is “nowise more divine nor more sacred than other diseases, but has a natural cause”, in the brain.
On the Sacred Disease says those who called epilepsy sacred used the gods as a screen for their own inability to cure it.
Hippocratic writings include case histories, and diagnosis and prognosis are frequent subjects in them.
The Hippocratic treatise On the Nature of Man (about 400 BCE) taught that health is a balance of four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.
The theory of the four humors was still current in Europe’s Middle Ages.
The Hippocratic Oath, from about 400 BCE, was probably not written by Hippocrates; revised versions are still used at many medical school graduations.
Doctors taking the Hippocratic Oath swore by Apollo and other gods to give only beneficial treatment and to keep patients’ secrets.

title: Democritus and the first atoms
description: Leucippus and Democritus argued that everything is made of indivisible atoms moving in the void.

facts.text: Leucippus and his pupil Democritus, a citizen of Abdera born about 460 BCE, developed the theory of atoms.
Democritus’s atoms were too small to be divided, hence the name atomon, “indivisible” or uncuttable.
For the atomists, everything is made of countless atoms moving through the void, an empty space.
Atoms differ only in shape, arrangement, position and size; water and iron differ by how their atoms are arranged.
Aristotle compared atoms to letters: A differs from N in shape, AN from NA in arrangement, and N from Z in position.
Democritus: “by convention sweet and by convention bitter, by convention hot, by convention cold, by convention color; but in reality atoms and void.”
The atoms seemed far too small to perceive, so no one could look at one to check the theory.
Aristotle rejected atomism, refusing to believe that all of reality comes down to atoms.

title: Greek maps of the world
description: Greek mapmaking ran from Anaximander’s world map to Eratosthenes’ grid and Ptolemy’s latitudes and longitudes.

facts.text: Anaximander of Miletus (about 610 to 546 BCE) drew a map of the known world, later corrected by his fellow Milesian Hecataeus.
Anaximander pictured Earth as a cylinder one-third as thick as it is wide, with people on its flat top, held up by nothing.
Eratosthenes invented geography as a discipline, creating its terms and probably the word geographia itself.
Eratosthenes’ Geographika placed some 400 places, from Thoule (probably Iceland) to Taprobane (Sri Lanka), on a grid of parallels and meridians.
Ptolemy’s Geography, from the 2nd century CE, gave latitudes and longitudes in degrees for about 8,000 places.
Ptolemy’s Geography was translated into Latin between 1406 and 1409, and its latitude and longitude grid gave Renaissance mapmakers a framework.

title: Greek inventions
description: Greek inventors built water clocks, pumps, the steam-spun aeolipile and the water mill.

facts.text: Ctesibius of Alexandria (about 270 BCE) improved the water clock: water dripping at a steady rate raised a float holding a pointer that marked the hours.
Ctesibius also invented force pumps and a water organ, in which the weight of water forced air through the pipes.
Hero of Alexandria (about 62 CE) described the aeolipile, a sphere spun by steam escaping from two bent nozzles, used to power toys and amuse visitors.
Hero’s aeolipile is counted as the first steam-powered engine.
Hero’s Pneumatica describes coin-operated machines, singing birds and a fire engine.
One of the oldest references to a water mill is a Greek poem celebrating that it freed the young women who ground grain in hand mills from their toil.
Easy to build and able to run in any fast stream, the water mill spread from Greece and was used throughout Europe by the end of the 3rd century CE.

title: Greek reason and nature
description: Greek thinkers studied nature by proof, measurement and argument, and prized proof above practical invention.

facts.text: Archimedes proved a sphere has two-thirds the volume of the cylinder around it, and asked for a sphere in a cylinder on his tomb.
Cicero found Archimedes’ tomb, overgrown with plants, about a century and a half after his death.
According to Plutarch, Archimedes thought so little of practical inventions that he left no written work on them.

title: The City Dionysia
description: Athens staged its plays as contests at the City Dionysia, a spring festival for Dionysus, whose image was brought in to watch.

facts.text: Athens held its drama contests at the City Dionysia, the spring festival of the god Dionysus, in the Theatre of Dionysus on the Acropolis’s south slope.
On festival days the image of Dionysus was carried from his nearby temple into the theater so that the god could be present at the plays.
At the City Dionysia each chosen tragic poet entered three tragedies and a satyr play, and a panel of judges picked the winner.
Admission to the Athenian theater was at first free; when a charge was later introduced, poor citizens were given the entrance money.

title: Parts of a Greek theater
description: Greek theaters set seats on a hillside around a round dancing floor, with a stage building behind; the words theater, orchestra and scene come from them.

facts.text: Greek theaters grew out of a flat performance area set before a natural hill, where the spectators sat on the slope.
Theater comes from Greek theatron, “a place of seeing”; the orchestra was the flat, round dancing place, and actors dressed in the skene, a small tent that gave us “scene”.
The theater at Epidaurus, built in the late 4th century BCE on a mountainside, is famed for its acoustics and still stages ancient drama at a summer festival.

title: How a Greek tragedy worked
description: Tragedy grew from a chorus: Thespis became the first actor, Aeschylus added a second and Sophocles a third, all men in masks, with plots from myth.

facts.text: Tradition credits Thespis, in the 6th century BCE, as the first actor to speak apart from the chorus; the word thespian comes from his name.
Aeschylus added a second actor and Sophocles a third, and a Greek tragedy never used more than three speaking actors.
All Greek actors were men and wore masks, which let them play women and switch between roles.
A tragic chorus of up to 15 men sang and danced.
Greek tragedies almost always took their plots from myth; audiences knew a myth’s outline but not which version a playwright would stage.

title: Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides
description: Three Athenian tragedians wrote about 300 plays; about 33 survive, and Euripides, least successful in life, survives best because his fame grew later.

facts.text: Aeschylus’s Oresteia (458 BCE), the only complete Greek trilogy to survive, opens with Agamemnon returning from the Trojan War and being murdered by his wife, Clytemnestra.
Aeschylus wrote about 90 plays and Sophocles about 123, and seven of each survive complete; Euripides wrote 92, and 19 survive counting one disputed: about 33 of some 300.
Euripides won only four first prizes in his lifetime, against perhaps 24 for Sophocles, but his fame later eclipsed his rivals’, so more of his plays survive.

title: Aristophanes and Old Comedy
description: Athenian Old Comedy, led by Aristophanes, mixed fantasy with open political satire of real people.

facts.text: Aristophanes wrote about 40 comedies, of which 11 survive; they are the chief examples of Athenian Old Comedy.
Old Comedy was full of political satire: Aristophanes attacked the politician Cleon in Knights (424 BCE) and mocked Socrates in Clouds (423 BCE).
In Aristophanes’s Lysistrata (411 BCE), the women of Athens and Sparta refuse sex until their husbands end the Peloponnesian War.
Aristophanes’s Frogs won first prize in 405 BCE: Dionysus goes to the underworld to bring back Euripides, judges a contest with Aeschylus, and brings back Aeschylus.

title: Menander and New Comedy
description: New Comedy, led by Menander, swapped politics for everyday life and stock characters; his plays were lost until papyrus finds.

facts.text: Menander (about 342–292 BCE), the greatest poet of New Comedy, wrote over 100 plays about everyday life, with stock characters like stern fathers, young lovers and scheming slaves.
Menander’s plays were long lost; the Dyskolos, about a grumpy old man and his only play to survive nearly complete, was first printed in 1958 from a papyrus found in Egypt.

title: The Greek lyre
description: The lyre, a stringed instrument with a tortoise-shell sound box, accompanied song and poetry and was part of Greek education; myth said Hermes invented it.

facts.text: The Greek lyre had two arms and a crossbar holding its strings; its common form, the chelys, had a sound box made from a tortoise shell.
In Greek myth, the baby god Hermes made the first lyre from a tortoise shell, stole Apollo’s cattle, and calmed Apollo by giving him the lyre.
The lyre was played alone or to accompany singing and poetry, and learning to play it was an integral part of Greek education.
