In the Odyssey, the blind singer Demodocus takes his lyre from a peg at the Phaeacian feast and sings of a quarrel between Odysseus and Achilles, while Odysseus hides his tears.

title: The aulos
description: The aulos was a reed pipe played in pairs, closer to an oboe than a flute, heard at the theater, in worship, at games and at drinking parties.

facts.text: The aulos was a reed pipe usually played in pairs, one pipe in each hand, and players often wore a leather strap across the cheeks.
The aulos is often translated “flute”, but as a reed instrument it sounded more like an oboe.
The aulos often accompanied choruses and played at the theater, in worship of Dionysus, at athletic contests and at drinking parties.

title: Greek lyric poetry
description: Lyric poetry, named for the lyre, was sung to it and often voiced personal feeling, in solo or choral songs.

facts.text: The word lyric comes from the lyre: Greek lyric poetry was performed to its accompaniment and often expressed personal emotion.
Greek lyric came in two kinds: solo songs by poets such as Sappho and Alcaeus, and choral songs by poets such as Pindar.

title: Sappho of Lesbos
description: Sappho, a lyric poet of Lesbos, was admired as the Tenth Muse, but her nine books are lost; we read her in one complete poem and papyrus fragments.

facts.text: Sappho lived about 610–570 BCE on the island of Lesbos and wrote about love, desire, weddings and the women of her circle; her style was admired in every age.
Scholars in Alexandria collected Sappho’s poems into nine books; that edition was lost by the early Middle Ages.
Only one of Sappho’s poems, an ode to Aphrodite, came down to us complete; the rest survives in quotations and papyrus fragments.
Many Sappho fragments come from papyri found at Oxyrhynchus, an ancient rubbish dump in Egypt, and some from the plaster-like wrapping of a mummy.
In 2004 scholars published papyrus that almost completed Sappho’s poem on old age, and in 2013 more fragments surfaced.
Ancient admirers called Sappho “the Tenth Muse”.

title: Greek sculpture comes to life
description: Greek statues moved from the stiff, frontal kouros to the relaxed weight shift (contrapposto) of the Kritios Boy.

facts.text: Archaic kouroi, stone statues of standing young men carved from about 615–590 BCE on, face stiffly forward with the left foot slightly forward and arms at their sides.
The Kritios Boy, a marble youth from the Athenian Acropolis made just after 480 BCE, rests his weight on his left leg with the right knee bent: an early contrapposto.

title: Lost bronzes and Roman copies
description: Most Greek bronze statues were melted down; we know many through Roman marble copies, and a few originals survived at sea.

facts.text: Polyclitus’s bronze Spear Bearer (Doryphoros), of about 450–440 BCE, is lost and known only through Roman copies.
Many Greek statues now known only in Roman marble copies were first made in bronze; the marble copies needed supports, often carved as tree trunks.
Full-size ancient Greek bronze statues rarely survive, because most were later melted down.
The Riace Bronzes, two Greek warriors probably made in the mid-5th century BCE, were found in the sea off southern Italy in 1972; they are among the few full-size Greek bronzes to survive.

title: Black-figure and red-figure
description: Black-figure painted black figures and scratched in details; red-figure, from about 530 BCE, painted the background black and brushed in details, freeing painters.

facts.text: In black-figure painting, which began in Corinth about 700 BCE, figures were painted black on the bare clay and details were scratched through the black.
Red-figure, invented in Athens about 530 BCE, reversed black-figure: the background was painted black, the figures left red, and details painted with a brush.
Brushed details gave red-figure painters more freedom to show bodies, movement and faces, and red-figure became the dominant style.

title: Pots with jobs
description: Greek pots did everyday work, like mixing wine; Panathenaic prize amphorae held olive oil and kept black-figure long after others dropped it.

facts.text: A krater was a large bowl for mixing wine with water.
Prize amphorae at Athens’s Panathenaic Games were filled with olive oil; one side showed Athena and the other the contest.
Panathenaic prize amphorae kept black-figure long after other pottery dropped it; one at Harvard dates to 340–339 BCE.

title: The three column orders
description: Greek columns come in three orders: plain Doric, scrolled Ionic and leafy Corinthian.

facts.text: Greek architecture has three orders: Doric (no base, a plain cushion-like capital), Ionic (a base and scrolls at the capital) and Corinthian (a capital of acanthus leaves).

title: Where the orders came from
description: Doric and Ionic grew up in wooden temples on opposite shores of the Aegean; Corinthian came last, wrapped in a Roman legend.

facts.text: The Doric and Ionic orders arose at nearly the same time on opposite shores of the Aegean: Doric on the Greek mainland, Ionic in the Greek cities of Asia Minor.
Both the Doric and the Ionic order began in temples built of wood.
The Roman architect Vitruvius said the Doric column was proportioned like a man and the Ionic like a woman, its scrolls like curling hair.
Vitruvius told how acanthus grew around a tile-covered basket left on a Corinthian girl’s grave, and the sculptor Callimachus based the Corinthian capital on it.
The Monument of Lysicrates in Athens, built in 334 BCE to celebrate a victory at the City Dionysia, has the earliest surviving Corinthian columns.

title: Herodotus
description: Herodotus inquired into the Greco-Persian Wars and their cause, recording what people told him, and became the father of history.

facts.text: Herodotus, born about 484 BCE in Halicarnassus in Asia Minor, wrote the first great narrative history of the ancient world, on the Greco-Persian Wars, and is called the father of history.
Herodotus opens his work as “the display of the inquiry” made so that “things done by man not be forgotten in time”, including the cause of the war.
Herodotus traveled widely, including to Egypt, and recorded peoples’ traditions without endorsing all of them, which earned him a reputation for believing too much.

title: Thucydides
description: Thucydides, an Athenian general who lived through the Peloponnesian War, wrote its history for accuracy, as a possession for all time.

facts.text: Thucydides, an Athenian, caught the plague of 430–429 BCE, was exiled for 20 years after failing to save Amphipolis as a general in 424 BCE, and wrote a history of the Peloponnesian War that breaks off in 411 BCE.
Thucydides wrote that the absence of romance might make his history less appealing, but he wrote it “as a possession for all time”, not to win the applause of the moment.

title: How Greek arts survived
description: Which Greek plays, poems and statues we have depended on later taste and luck: copied manuscripts, Egyptian papyri, shipwrecks and Roman copies.

facts.text: Greek plays, poems and statues reached us by different routes: texts later readers kept copying, papyri found in Egypt, bronzes lost at sea and Roman copies.

title: Philip of Macedon
description: Philip II, once a hostage in Thebes, rebuilt Macedonia’s army around the long sarissa, beat Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE and led the Greeks until his murder in 336 BCE.

facts.text: As a young man, Philip of Macedonia spent about three years, from around 367 BCE, as a hostage in Thebes, where he studied under the great general Epaminondas.
Philip became king of Macedonia in 359 BCE, at the age of 23.
Philip armed his soldiers with the sarissa, a pike roughly twice as long as the spear of the Greeks.
In 338 BCE, at Chaeronea, Philip defeated the combined armies of Athens and Thebes.
Philip’s son Alexander, only 18, commanded the left wing at Chaeronea.
In 337 BCE Philip organized the Greek states into the League of Corinth, with himself as its leader, and planned a war against Persia.
In 336 BCE Philip was stabbed to death by his bodyguard Pausanias in the theater at Aegae, during celebrations of his daughter’s wedding.
Alexander, born in 356 BCE, became king in 336 BCE, at the age of 20.

title: Alexander’s education
description: Aristotle taught Alexander from 13 to 16; Alexander treasured the Iliad and claimed Achilles as an ancestor.

facts.text: From age 13 to 16, Alexander was taught by the philosopher Aristotle, who inspired his interest in philosophy, medicine and scientific investigation.
Plutarch writes that Philip sent for Aristotle, ’the most famous and learned of philosophers’, and gave teacher and pupil the precinct of the nymphs near Mieza as their school.
According to Plutarch, Philip paid Aristotle by rebuilding his hometown, Stageira, which Philip had destroyed, and bringing back its citizens from exile or slavery.
Plutarch writes that Alexander called the Iliad a handbook of the art of war, and kept Aristotle’s edition of it, the ’Iliad of the Casket’, under his pillow with his dagger.
Plutarch says that on his mother’s side Alexander descended from Neoptolemus, the son of Achilles.

title: Bucephalus
description: Plutarch tells how young Alexander tamed Bucephalus by turning him away from his shadow; the horse died in India and a city was named after him.

facts.text: Plutarch tells that a horse dealer offered Bucephalus to Philip for 13 talents; the horse seemed wild and unmanageable until Alexander saw it was frightened by its own shadow and turned it toward the sun.
In Plutarch’s story, Philip told his son: ’seek thee out a kingdom equal to thyself; Macedonia has not room for thee.’
The name Bucephalus is Greek for ’bull-headed’.
Bucephalus died, aged 30, after Alexander’s battle against Porus on the Hydaspes River in 326 BCE, and Alexander founded a city there named Bucephala after him.
Alexander founded several cities named Alexandria, from Egypt to Central Asia.

title: How we know about Alexander
description: The surviving accounts of Alexander were written centuries later by Plutarch and Arrian, from eyewitness histories now lost.

facts.text: The main surviving accounts of Alexander, by Plutarch and Arrian, were written about four centuries after he died; the eyewitness histories they used, like that of Callisthenes, are lost.
Plutarch was born around 46 CE in Chaeronea.

title: Alexander conquers Persia
description: From 334 to 330 BCE Alexander beat the Persians at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, took Tyre and Egypt, and burned Persepolis.

facts.text: In spring 334 BCE Alexander crossed the Dardanelles into Asia with about 30,000 infantry and more than 5,000 cavalry.
Before his first battle in Asia, Alexander visited Troy, where, Plutarch says, he anointed the gravestone of Achilles with oil and ran a race by it with his companions.
In 334 BCE Alexander won his first battle against a Persian army at the Granicus River.
In 333 BCE Alexander defeated the Persian king Darius III at Issus, and Darius fled.
Legend said whoever loosed the Gordian knot would rule Asia; most ancient writers say Alexander cut it with his sword, but the story may be apocryphal.
In 332 BCE Alexander stormed the island city of Tyre after a siege, and Egypt surrendered to him without a real fight.
In 331 BCE Alexander defeated Darius at Gaugamela, the decisive battle of the war.
In 330 BCE Alexander burned the palace of Xerxes at Persepolis as a sign that the Greek war of revenge on Persia was over, and Darius was stabbed by a usurper among his own men.

title: Alexander in India
description: Alexander crossed the Indus in 326 BCE and beat Porus on the Hydaspes, but his army refused to go past the Hyphasis, and the return through Gedrosia was a disaster.

facts.text: In Central Asia Alexander captured Roxana, daughter of a local noble, and married her to make peace.
In spring 326 BCE Alexander crossed the Indus and entered India.
In 326 BCE Alexander defeated King Porus on the Hydaspes River; Porus’s elephants were unfamiliar to the Macedonians.
Plutarch writes that when Alexander asked the captured Porus how he wished to be treated, Porus answered ’like a king’; impressed, Alexander kept him as ruler and gave him more land.
At the Hyphasis River, Alexander’s army mutinied and refused to go any farther; Alexander, Plutarch says, shut himself in his tent in anger before giving in.
At the Hyphasis, Alexander set up 12 altars to the 12 Olympian gods.
On the way back, Alexander’s march through the Gedrosian desert was a disaster of thirst and hunger; Plutarch wrote that not even a quarter of his fighting force came back from India.

title: Alexander’s death and the Successors
description: Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE with no adult heir; his family was killed off and his generals fought over the empire until 281 BCE.

facts.text: Alexander fell ill after a long banquet and drinking bout in Babylon and died 10 days later, on June 13, 323 BCE, aged 32.
What killed Alexander is still debated: the most popular theories are malaria, typhoid fever and poison, though Plutarch thought the poison story a fabrication.
The historian Diodorus writes that the dying Alexander gave his ring to his general Perdiccas and, asked who should have his kingdom, answered ’to the strongest’.
Alexander had named no heir, so his generals made two kings: his half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus and his son by Roxana, Alexander IV, born after his death.
In 310 BCE the general Cassander had the boy king Alexander IV and his mother Roxana killed.
Alexander’s generals, the Successors, fought over his empire from 323 to 281 BCE.

title: The Hellenistic kingdoms
description: After Ipsus in 301 BCE, Alexander’s empire settled into kingdoms ruled by Macedonian families: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Asia and the Antigonids in Macedonia.

facts.text: Seleucus, one of Alexander’s generals, gave up territory to the Indian ruler Chandragupta in exchange for 500 elephants.
At Ipsus in 301 BCE, Seleucus and his allies beat Antigonus, who was killed; Seleucus’s estimated 400 elephants made the difference, and hopes of reuniting Alexander’s empire ended.
The Ptolemies, descended from Alexander’s general Ptolemy, ruled Egypt as kings from 305 BCE until 30 BCE.
The Seleucid kingdom at its greatest stretched from Thrace to the border of India; its main capital was Antioch in Syria, and Rome ended it in 64 BCE.
The Antigonid family, descended from Alexander’s general Antigonus, ruled Macedonia from 306 to 168 BCE.
In the Hellenistic kingdoms Greek became the language of government, and Greek culture mixed with the cultures of the peoples the kings ruled.

title: Alexandria’s Library and Lighthouse
description: The Ptolemies’ Library of Alexandria set out to collect every book, mostly Greek, and the Greek-built Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders.

facts.text: About 295 BCE, Ptolemy I had Demetrius of Phaleron found the library and the Mouseion in Alexandria, aiming to collect, if possible, all the books in the world.
Demetrius of Phaleron was an Athenian statesman and philosopher who became prominent at the court of Ptolemy I.
Most of the Library of Alexandria’s books were in Greek.
Ptolemy III borrowed Athens’ official copies of the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, leaving 15 talents of silver as security, then kept the originals and returned copies.
The scholar Callimachus, who worked at the library, compiled the Pinakes, a catalog of its authors and their works by field of learning, in 120 books.
The lighthouse on the island of Pharos was built by Sostratus of Cnidus, a Greek architect, and finished about 280 BCE.
The Lighthouse of Alexandria rose more than 110 metres, had a fire burning at the top at night, and was one of the Seven Wonders of the World.

title: Rome conquers Greece
description: Rome ended Macedonia’s kingdom at Pydna in 168 BCE and destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE, but Greek culture won over the Romans.

facts.text: In 168 BCE Rome defeated King Perseus of Macedonia at Pydna, ending the Antigonid kingdom.
After Pydna, Polybius was one of 1,000 leading Achaeans deported to Rome as hostages.

In Rome Polybius became a friend of the general Scipio Aemilianus and wrote his Histories, in Greek, to explain how the Romans had brought nearly the whole inhabited world under their rule in under 53 years.
When Rome destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE, most of its men were killed and its women and children were enslaved.
The Roman general Mummius shipped Corinth’s art treasures to Rome and warned the shippers that anything lost or damaged would have to be replaced with work of equal value.
The Roman poet Horace wrote that captive Greece took her fierce conqueror captive and brought the arts to rustic Latium.

title: Greek culture from Egypt to India
description: Alexander’s conquests planted Greek cities as far as Afghanistan and made Greek a common language across the East.

facts.text: Ai Khanoum, in northern Afghanistan, was a Greek city founded in the wake of Alexander’s conquests, with a gymnasium and a theater.

At Ai Khanoum a man named Clearchus set up Delphic sayings he had copied: ’As a child, be orderly; as a youth, self-controlled; as an adult, just; as an old man, of good counsel; when dying, without sorrow.’

Koine, the common Greek of the Hellenistic age, was used from Greece and Macedonia to the Greek-ruled parts of Africa and the Middle East until the 6th century CE; the New Testament was written in it.

title: Greek in English words
description: Everyday English words such as telephone, photograph, school and dinosaur are built from ancient Greek parts, often coined in modern times.

facts.text: Telephone comes from Greek tele, "far", and phone, "sound, voice"; the word was coined around 1830 for a system that sent words using musical notes.
In 1839 John Herschel coined photograph from Greek photo-, "light", and -graph, "something written".
School comes, through Latin, from Greek skhole, "leisure" or "spare time", which came to mean learned discussion and then a place for it.
In the 1840s the anatomist Richard Owen coined dinosaur from Greek deinos, "terrible", and sauros, "lizard".

title: Democracy then and now
description: Athenian democracy was direct but limited to adult male citizens; modern democracies are mostly representative and, as Madison argued, suited to large countries.

facts.text: Democracy comes from Greek demos, "people", and kratos, "rule".
In Athens, citizens voted on laws themselves in the Assembly; most democracies today are representative, with voters electing lawmakers.
Only adult male citizens could take part in Athenian democracy; women, slaves and foreigners were excluded, so most inhabitants had no vote.
In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to let women vote in national elections.

In Federalist No. 10 (1787), James Madison called a pure democracy a small number of citizens who assemble and govern in person, and argued a republic, run by elected representatives, could cover a far larger country.

title: The modern Olympics
description: Pierre de Coubertin’s revival brought the Olympics back in Athens in 1896, with new traditions such as the marathon and, from 1936, the torch relay.

facts.text: The French educator Pierre de Coubertin led the revival of the Olympics: in 1894 a congress at the Sorbonne in Paris agreed to hold international Games and founded the International Olympic Committee.
The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896.

The marathon was a new race at the 1896 Games, inspired by the legend of a runner carrying news from Marathon to Athens; the Greek Spyridon Louis won it by more than seven minutes and became a national hero.

The Olympic torch relay began with the 1936 Berlin Games in Nazi Germany: a flame lit at Olympia with a mirror focusing the Sun’s rays was carried by runners to Berlin. Ancient Greeks never ran such a relay.

title: The Greek Revival
description: In the 19th century architects copied Greek temples for banks and memorials, from Philadelphia’s Second Bank to the Lincoln Memorial.

facts.text: The Greek Revival, a style based on 5th-century-BCE Greek temples, spread through Europe and the United States in the first half of the 19th century; the Parthenon was a favorite model.
William Strickland designed the Second Bank of the United States in Philadelphia, built 1819 to 1824, taking the Parthenon as his model for its columns and plain pediments.
Henry Bacon modeled the Lincoln Memorial, dedicated in 1922, on the Parthenon, feeling a memorial to a man who defended democracy should echo democracy’s birthplace.
The Lincoln Memorial has 36 columns, one for each state in the Union when Lincoln died.

title: Myths retold
description: Greek myths live on in modern books and films, from Joyce’s Ulysses to Percy Jackson, and retellers have always added details, like Achilles’ heel.

facts.text: James Joyce’s novel Ulysses (1922), set in Dublin on one day, June 16, 1904, is built as a modern parallel to Homer’s Odyssey, with Leopold Bloom as Odysseus.
Ulysses is the name Odysseus goes by in English, from the Latin form of his name.
For the 1963 film Jason and the Argonauts, stop-motion animator Ray Harryhausen spent four months on a battle between Jason, two Argonauts and an army of skeletons.
In Rick Riordan’s 2005 novel The Lightning Thief, Percy Jackson learns he is a son of Poseidon, and the gods’ Mount Olympus sits on the 600th floor of the Empire State Building.
The story that Thetis dipped the baby Achilles in the River Styx, leaving only the heel she held vulnerable, is not in Homer; it was added by later tellers.

title: Science’s Greek roots
description: Modern science still uses Greek words, letters and ideas: the "uncuttable" atom, Rutherford’s alpha and beta rays, and the doctors’ oath descended from Hippocrates.

facts.text: Atom comes from Greek atomos, "uncuttable" or "indivisible", from an ancient Greek idea that matter is made of tiny pieces that cannot be divided.
In 1897 the English physicist J. J. Thomson discovered the electron, the first known particle smaller than an atom.

In 1899 Ernest Rutherford found radioactive substances give off more than one kind of radiation and named the less penetrating rays alpha and the more penetrating ones beta, after the first two Greek letters.
The Hippocratic oath is an ethical code attributed to the Greek physician Hippocrates; versions of it still appear in the graduation ceremonies of many medical schools.
In 1948 the World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Geneva, known as the modern version of the Hippocratic oath.

title: How Greek books survived
description: Greek texts survived through Byzantine copies, Arabic translations in Baghdad and manuscripts carried to Italy, sometimes by luck, as with the Archimedes Palimpsest.

facts.text: The Venetus A, made toward the end of the 10th century CE, more than 1,500 years after Homer, is the oldest complete text of the Iliad.
In the 15th century the Greek cardinal Bessarion acquired the Venetus A and gave his whole collection of Greek manuscripts to Venice, where it remains.
In 9th-century Baghdad, Hunayn ibn Ishaq (808-873) translated works of Plato, Aristotle, Hippocrates and Galen from Greek.
Most of Galen’s original Greek manuscripts were lost, and some of his works survive only in Arabic translation.
After Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, Byzantine refugees brought more Greek manuscripts to the West, and older Latin translations made from Arabic versions came to seem inadequate.

A Byzantine copy of works by Archimedes was scraped and written over with prayers in the 13th century; spotted in 1906 and recovered with modern imaging, it holds the only surviving copy of his Method.

title: Myths about Greece
description: Greek statues and temple sculptures were painted, not plain white, and the Greeks called themselves Hellenes; "Greek" is a Roman name.

facts.text: Ancient Greek sculptures were painted in bright colors (polychromy); researchers detect surviving pigment traces with infrared and ultraviolet light and build colored reconstructions.
A 2023 study found traces of Egyptian blue, white and purple paint on the Parthenon Sculptures in the British Museum.
Most paint on Greek sculptures wore away over time, and restorers sometimes removed surviving traces to restore an assumed original whiteness.
The 18th-century art historian Johann Joachim Winckelmann linked whiteness with beauty, writing that color should play a minor part in it.
The ancient Greeks called themselves Hellenes; the name Greek comes from Latin Graeci, the Romans’ name for them.
One theory traces Graeci to Greeks from Graia, a town in Boeotia, who helped found Cumae in Italy, where Romans first met Greeks.
Greece’s official name today is the Hellenic Republic.

title: Why Greece still matters
description: Admiration for ancient Greece shaped modern history, from Shelley’s "We are all Greeks" to Greek independence, though Greece also borrowed and passed on others’ ideas.

facts.text: In the preface to Hellas (1822), a poem inspired by the Greek War of Independence, Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote: "We are all Greeks. Our laws, our literature, our religion, our arts have their root in Greece."
The Greek War of Independence against Ottoman rule began in 1821, and in 1830 the London protocol made Greece an independent state.
The poet Lord Byron went to Greece to help its fight for independence, died of fever at Missolonghi in 1824, and became a Greek national hero.
